newsitem.title: RWANDA: 21 people, most of them children, killed in Rwanda.
newsitem.headline: 21 people, most of them children, killed in Rwanda.

text.p: Unidentified gunmen in eastern Rwanda killed 21 Hutus, most of them children, who had returned late last year from Tanzania, neighbours said on Saturday.

The neighbours, who declined to be identified, said they heard screams and gunshots at about midnight on Thursday and in the morning found 11 dead at one house and 10 dead at another 150 metres (yards) away.
The 21 people -- five adults and 16 children -- had been shot dead. They were all Hutus, the majority ethnic group.
"We have no idea who could have done this. Nobody here saw anything," said a farmer who lived close to one of the houses.
Killings, particularly in western Rwanda, have increased since the return of more than a million Hutu refugees from camps in Tanzania and Zaire in the last two months of last year.
They fled in 1994, fearing reprisals for the genocide of 800,000 Tutsis and moderate Hutus by Hutu troops, militiamen and mobs.
The government has blamed recent attacks on Hutu extremists targeting minority Tutsis and those who witnessed the genocide to stop them giving evidence against suspects or identifying the killers.

The neighbours identified the victims as members of the Kabeza and Neza families who left Tanzania in December and returned to their homes among banana plantations on a hilltop near Kibungo, 100 km (60 miles) east of Rwanda's capital Kigali.
Neighbours said police came to investigate the killings. But local authorities were not immediately available for comment.

"They were refugees who came back from Tanzania with nothing to start farming again," said a student. The two houses were deserted on Saturday and reeked of stale blood. The dead -- five adults and 16 children -- had been buried.
Amnesty International said on Wednesday it estimated hundreds of people had been killed in Rwanda so far this year.
The London-based human rights group reported an increase in unlawful executions by the Tutsi-dominated Rwanda Patriotic Army (RPA) especially in the context of reprisal operations after attacks.
It also reported killings by armed groups believed to be Hutu former soldiers of the Hutu Rwandan army and Interahamwe militiamen who had a leading role in the 1994 mass slaughter.
It said Tutsi civilians were also killing Hutu civilians.
Defence Ministry spokesman Major Emmanuel Ndahiro said on state radio on Saturday the Amnesty report lacked information and analysis and depended on hearsay instead of first-hand information.
He said the RPA was not involved in unlawful executions.
Ndahiro said most acts of violence in Rwanda were by former Hutu soldiers and Interahamwe militiamen but he did not rule out that some civilians were caught in crossfire as troops pursued attackers.

Amnesty said at least 60 Hutu returnees from Tanzania were beaten to death by Tutsi civilians in two separate incidents in Rusomo in the eastern Kibungo region in mid-January and some of their bodies were reportedly dumped in ditches and latrines.
It said the killing of five U.N. human rights workers in the southwest on February 4 was preventing international and local agencies carrying out independent investigations into abuses.
